claims.statement: Mace agreed to fight Allen for $2,500 a side.
Mace proposed three places for the fight: in Virginia, in Canada within 100 miles of Montreal, or in Louisiana within 50 miles of New Orleans.
Tom Allen declined Joe Coburn's challenge to fight for $5,000 or $10,000.
Allen's promised articles for a match with Mace reached the New York Clipper on Monday, January 3, 1870 (printed as 'January 34').
Allen's articles proposed a fight with Mace for $2,500 a side and the championship of America.
Tom Allen reportedly telegraphed Jem Mace in New York accepting his challenge.
Tom Allen and Jem Mace signed articles on January 17, 1870 to fight for $10,000 and the championship of the world.
Tom Allen declined Joe Coburn's challenge to fight for $500 or $10,000 (printed as $10,009) until after his contest with Jim Mace in July.
A match between Tom Allen and Jem Mace was arranged, to be fought in the vicinity of Cincinnati next March.
James Mace wrote in a card that he would only whip Tom Allen for the reputation and battle-money of their meeting, with no international character to it.
Tom Allen challenged any man except Mace and Heenan to fight him for $500 to $5,000, naming Joe Coburn, Mike McCoole, Charley Gallagher and Joe Goss.
From New York, Tom Allen issued a challenge to all professional bruisers except Mace and Heenan.
Tom Allen challenged all professional bruisers except Mace and Heenan to fight for $3,000 or less.
Tom Allen was particularly anxious that Joe Coburn accept his challenge.
Tom Allen was soon to contest Mike McCoole for the championship of America.
Mike McCoole was said to be soon to contest Tom Allen for the championship, for $5,000 a side.
Tom Allen would not fight Coburn until after his contest with Jem Mace, expected in July 1870.
Tom Allen's contest with Jim Mace was expected to take place in July 1870.
Tom Allen intimated to his friends that he would not accept McCoole's last challenge to fight for the belts, saying he could not afford a month or two of training for a fight with no money to win.

Rumours from New York of a $1,000-a-side match between Tom Allen and Joe Goss of England, said to have been made by Joe Coburn and Jim Mace, were treated as moonshine; Allen said no match had been made and he had no information on the subject.
Billy Carroll, of Carroll's Sample room, tried to make a match between Mike McCoole and Tom Allen.
Mike McCoole issued a manifesto challenging Tom Allen to fight for the champion belt and the excursion money.
Tom Allen sent the New York Clipper a challenge to fight any man in America for $2,500 or $5,000 a side, Joe Coburn preferred.
If the challenge were accepted, the fight would take place at a point between St. Louis and a place the OCR cannot read.
The second deposit of $500 a side for the Tom Allen and McCoole match was not paid to Mr. Murray on July 1, 1870, and Roach, Allen's representative, claimed the stakes already deposited.
A total of $1,000 had been deposited for the Tom Allen and McCoole match.
Allen's articles proposed that the fight take place within fifty miles of Cincinnati on July 5, 1870.
Allen proposed to fight Jem Mace for $2,500 a side on 5 July 1870, within fifty miles of a place the OCR garbles as 'vane', with the forfeit lost by any party arrested in another state.
The fight with Mace was also to be, as alleged by Billy Carroll, for the championship of the world.
Tom Allen and James C. Gallagher signed articles of agreement at Hennessy's saloon for a match.
Tom Allen and Jas. C. Gallagher made a match for a fight at a meeting over Hennessey's saloon, Fourth and Morgan streets.
The match was for $1,500, with Allen staking $1,000 against Gallagher's $500.
Allen deposited $200 and Gallagher deposited $100 toward the match.
The last deposit was $200 for Allen and $100 for Gallagher.
Gallagher proposed fighting Tom Allen in Louisiana, Kansas, Arkansas or Kentucky, and Allen said he would fight in any of these places.
Immediately after that exhibition, Jack Leoney offered $5,000 to back Tom Allen in a match.
Tom Allen wrote from St. Louis, in a letter dated January 1871, that he had challenged Joe Coburn ten times and that Coburn never answered.

Allen offered to give Joe Coburn $200 to withdraw from his match with Jem Mace, and to stake $3,000 to fight Coburn on the same day, the 11th of April (printed as '1th of A:'), about fifty miles from Detroit.
A New York dispatch of May 14, 1871 reported that Tom Allen offered to fight Joe Coburn for $5,000 (printed as $5020) or Ned O'Baldwin for $1,000 a side.
A New York dispatch of May 14, 1871 reported that Tom Allen offered to fight Joe Coburn for $5,000 or Ned O'Baldwin for $1,090 (printed as $1,090).
Tom Allen denied the dispatch that he had challenged Joe Coburn and Ned O'Baldwin, and said he had given no such challenge and had no intention of doing so.
Mike McCoole was reported to want a match with Tom Allen.
Tom Allen challenged Mike McCoole once more, about two years after the Mace fight, and McCoole accepted.
Billy Carroll published a card offering to back Mike McCoole in a match against Tom Allen.
Tom Allen offered to fight Joe Coburn for $2,500 or $5,000 as an alternative to McCoole.
Tom Allen answered with a conditional offer to meet Carroll at the St. Louis Billiard Hall on Monday, January 8, 1872, and put up $500 to fight McCoole.
Several friends of Tom Kelly offered to back him with $500 or more to fight Tom Allen, if Allen could be brought down to Kelly's weight.
A rumour said a match between Tom Kelly and Tom Allen was being arranged, but no definite steps had been taken.
